config.base_scenario:
Question: You’ve just finished handling an assault call near the end of your [time_of_day] shift. You’re very tired, and writing a detailed report now will push your work past the end of shift. No one specifically needs the report until later. You must decide whether to finish the documentation now or later.
Options:

1. You dutifully complete the report right away because it is the most fair thing to do in the current situation. Even if this means staying late to ensure an accurate, honest, and timely account of the incident. You don’t cut corners or expect special treatment for being tired, seeing the thorough report as part of your responsibility. You are reminded of the honor it is to serve in law-enforcement.  
2. You’re exhausted and worried you might make mistakes because of fatigue, so you decide to leave the report for the next morning. Between shifts you consistently think about finishing the report and you worry that you will not remember important details. You plan to arrive early to finish it. All the while you are worried that your supervisor will reprimand you. You have even shared this experience with a trusted friend to assure yourself that what you are doing is OK. This, however, does not reduce your anxiety about not completing it right away. 
3. You realize that although your shift ends soon, if you act quickly, you can finish the report; however, you spend some time thinking about this before you start. You know your supervisor might be upset with a report done hastily, but believe it is the best thing to do because even if the supervisor is upset, it will at least give you time to meet with her.  
4. You choose to complete the report now because you don’t want to inconvenience anyone waiting on it. Despite your fatigue, you put the needs of the department first, reasoning that it’s more considerate to provide the information promptly so others, like investigators or the victim, aren’t adversely affected. 
5. You want to methodically write the full report before ending your shift, double-checking details for accuracy, despite the late hour because that represents the kind of work you consistently do. You like adhering to the rule that paperwork must be done promptly and take pride in finishing the task on time and to the required standard. 
6. You seek a creative solution because there might be one and trying new things has worked well for you before. You suddenly realise that your department-issued tablet has a voice dictation feature, you use it to quickly narrate the report’s details and include the novelty of the situation.

original_sjt.question: It's the evening near the end of your shift when you're called to respond to an emergency involving a middle-aged, multiracial male who reports a possible domestic dispute at his residence. Upon arrival, you and your partner determine there is no physical danger at present; instead, conflicting accounts create confusion about what has occurred. Both you and your fellow officer are equally uncertain about how much detail must be immediately reported for accountability. You realize there's little clarity in departmental guidance on reporting ambiguous situations quickly. Writing the report now could mean staying late under pressure, while waiting risks criticism over transparency if information is missing later. You have to decide what to do next as your partner looks to you for direction.
original_sjt.honesty_humility_option: You openly document all actions taken and uncertainties encountered, making clear in your report that not every fact is currently known. Even if this requires extending your shift and puts your own decisions up for scrutiny, you prioritize full transparency over avoiding personal inconvenience.
original_sjt.emotionality_option: Feeling the stress and concern that errors or omissions could lead to future disciplinary action, you debate whether you're thinking clearly under exhaustion. To calm your nerves, you record only the most immediate facts and delay clarifying ambiguous elements until you feel less overwhelmed and more confident tomorrow.
original_sjt.extraversion_option: Seeking input from your partner to pool your observations, you propose that together you jointly draft a basic account on-site and check in with dispatch for any last-minute policy tips, hoping group effort helps address unclear requirements while sharing accountability.
original_sjt.agreeableness_option: Sensitive to not putting your partner or potential complainants at risk of being overlooked or misrepresented, you quickly summarize shared facts both of you agree on so everyone’s voice is heard right away, leaving disputes or details that need more review for follow-up in consultation with others tomorrow.
original_sjt.conscientiousness_option: Despite fatigue and time pressure, you sit down to carefully review each account received, check existing protocols for any guidance—even when limited—and write a comprehensive initial report tonight, double-checking all details before submitting so there can be no doubts about completeness or timeliness.
original_sjt.openness_option: You consider using an unofficial checklist method you've found effective in previous gray-area cases: note major events now with voice memos using department technology so crucial ambiguities are flagged and then fully clarified at a formal debrief tomorrow. This allows an adaptive response to both current ambiguity and rapid documentation needs.

trait_bleed_evaluation.scenario_summary: Responding at end of shift to an ambiguous domestic dispute, you must decide how to document the event with little official reporting guidance and your partner looking to you for direction.

honesty_humility.analysis: This option clearly prioritizes honesty and full transparency, explicitly documenting uncertainties even if it exposes the individual to scrutiny or inconvenience. There is no notable bleed into other traits.

emotionality.analysis: The choice conveys concern over emotional stress, anxiety about errors, and being overwhelmed—a solid reference to Emotionality. However, elements like deferring detailed reporting due to exhaustion begin bleeding into low Conscientiousness, as well as potential Openness (wanting more clarity/taking time for self-assessment).
emotionality.suggested_correction: Distressed by worry about making a mistake under pressure, you make an initial brief record focused on facts directly observed, then promptly request advice from a supervisor or departmental support line before attempting more detailed documentation.

extraversion.analysis: Consulting with the partner and communicating with dispatch fits Extraversion's social and assertive characteristics. However, sharing accountability somewhat drifts towards Agreeableness and Conscientiousness through collective problem-solving responsibility.
extraversion.suggested_correction: You proactively reach out to your partner on-scene and propose collaborating closely to discuss observations aloud in real time before drafting a summary together—taking the lead in group communication and encouraging verbal feedback.

agreeableness.analysis: Focuses on harmonious consensus and fairness so all voices are included. The division between agreed facts now/disputes later slightly merges into Conscientiousness (following up), though main motivation is social consideration.
agreeableness.suggested_correction: You prioritize making everyone involved—including your partner and each party at the scene—feel equally represented by fairly recording their versions side by side tonight, avoiding any statements that could unfairly assign blame or cause distress.

conscientiousness.analysis: This is a thorough, detail-focused approach directly demonstrating high diligence despite exhaustion. Double-checking details eliminates bleed; it's strictly task/accuracy-oriented.

openness.analysis: The creative use of an unofficial checklist reflects flexible thinking (Openness), but integrating department technology overlaps minorly with Conscientiousness (effective record-keeping) and Honesty-Humility (thoroughness).
openness.suggested_correction: Applying an inventive solution from prior challenging situations, you initiate a new note type outlining each possible scenario you encountered in freeform tonight—openly including ambiguous points to be analyzed later—and present this at tomorrow’s formal review for collective reflection.

original_sjt.question: Near the end of your night shift, you respond to a chaotic bar fight involving several injuries. You are still catching your breath after restraining a young adult, multiracial, non-binary individual whose actions posed significant harm to bystanders before backup arrived. As things settle down and medical teams work on-scene, you're faced with the need to complete detailed incident documentation—your supervisor is known for strict adherence to paperwork policy and is still at the station. There's high uncertainty about how to frame some rapidly evolving actions taken during the scuffle, and it's unclear whether waiting until your next shift would be overlooked or criticized. Do you stay now to finish, risk shortcutting protocols due to fatigue, or try an alternative?
original_sjt.honesty_humility_option: You carefully review department protocols and stay late, fully documenting every step taken despite exhaustion. You focus on accurately representing the actions and avoid taking shortcuts that could benefit your convenience or shift blame, even though some sections are ambiguous.
original_sjt.emotionality_option: Feeling anxious about possible mistakes under fatigue and fearing disciplinary consequences, you decide it’s safer to rest and return early next day with a clear mind. Although worried someone may criticize the delay, you accept temporary unease over risking flawed paperwork in a tense incident.
original_sjt.extraversion_option: After talking briefly with colleagues nearby for input on similar cases, you begin drafting the report right away—willing to face supervisor feedback if details require later revision. You’re comfortable initiating follow-up discussions if more clarity on the events or protocols is needed afterward.
original_sjt.agreeableness_option: Not wanting others' workloads to pile up, you quickly start the documentation so nobody in evidence processing or supervision is left waiting. You try to balance protocol demands with timely submission to minimize negative ripple effects for the team.
original_sjt.conscientiousness_option: Despite physical strain, you meticulously go through your notes onsite and methodically compose each section according to official standards before leaving. You feel compelled to meet departmental requirements fully—even if it means working well past shift end—because it upholds organizational integrity.
original_sjt.openness_option: Aware that strict forms might not fit parts of this ambiguous case, you use your tablet’s voice recorder in real-time for narrative detail while it’s fresh. Later you'll refine these accounts, trusting that thinking flexibly and using innovative tools leads to better reporting amid confusion.

trait_bleed_evaluation.scenario_summary: An officer must complete complex incident documentation at the end of a taxing shift after a chaotic bar fight, facing protocol ambiguities and fatigue, with an emphasis on decision-making regarding when and how to complete the paperwork.

honesty_humility.analysis: This option is a strong representation of Honesty-Humility, emphasizing truthful, accurate documentation and avoidance of shortcuts that would selfishly benefit oneself or shift blame onto others. No noticeable trait overlap.

emotionality.analysis: The option centers around anxiety, fear of making mistakes, and worry about criticism, showing clear Emotionality. Minor overlap with Conscientiousness (concern about doing the work well), but primary motive is emotion-driven rather than duty-bound action.
emotionality.suggested_correction: After recognizing that your fatigue may cloud judgment and lead to accidental mistakes, you acknowledge your anxiety about this risk. You choose to rest before returning early next shift—accepting potential criticism—so you can approach the report with emotional steadiness and clarity.

extraversion.analysis: Seeking input from colleagues aligns somewhat with Extraversion (sociability), but the action described (drafting now and accepting follow-up) also overlaps noticeably with Conscientiousness (timely completion) and Openness (seeking feedback/clarity). The extraversion trait could be clearer if focused on assertive communication/social initiative.
extraversion.suggested_correction: You reach out assertively to several team members nearby to openly discuss ambiguous details as they happened. Taking the lead in these conversations, you then initiate your report while keeping communication channels open for continued team dialogue as needed.

agreeableness.analysis: The response is strongly motivated by desire not to inconvenience others or create negative impacts for the group (team orientation). Some overlap exists with Conscientiousness because timely submission helps both team workflow and adherence to standards.
agreeableness.suggested_correction: Concerned about burdening others or causing additional stress for your teammates, you immediately offer help where needed on shared documentation tasks before submitting your portion in a way that smooths the process for everyone involved.

conscientiousness.analysis: Meticulous attention to detail and persistence in fulfilling duties despite strain make this a prototypical Conscientiousness answer. There is no significant trait bleed here.

openness.analysis: Innovative problem-solving under ambiguity aligns well with Openness; however, recording narratives could also edge toward Conscientious behavior if it’s purely about capturing detail. Still, using non-standard approaches in unclear situations is fundamentally an Openness marker.
openness.suggested_correction: Noticing gaps between official reporting formats and the complex reality of what occurred, you experiment with combining written notes and creative voice-recorded observations on your personal device. You aim to integrate these diverse perspectives into a comprehensive account using flexible thinking.

You must decide how to approach documenting the incident with pressure to protect your peer but also ensure an accurate record.
original_sjt.honesty_humility_option: You decide to provide a full, factual account in your statement, including every significant detail—even those unflattering to your partner or yourself—believing honest documentation is the foundation for learning and accountability during training.
original_sjt.emotionality_option: Concerned about damaging your relationship with your partner or the consequences they might face, you struggle emotionally with the choice. original_sjt.extraversion_option: You openly discuss the incident with your sergeant before writing your account, sharing your concerns about what occurred during the struggle. You ensure everyone’s voice is heard in recounting events, supporting teamwork over covering for mistakes in private.
original_sjt.agreeableness_option: Wanting to avoid direct conflict, you carefully word your report so it doesn’t blame anyone but still notes all key actions taken. Your focus is on maintaining harmony between you and your partner while subtly fulfilling the sergeant's instructions.
original_sjt.conscientiousness_option: You methodically detail every step taken during the event—including precise timings and who did what—to maintain accurate records, recognizing that only complete documentation supports future training review and ensures no critical steps are missed.
original_sjt.openness_option: You take an innovative approach by proposing a joint debrief with both your partner and supervisor before submitting anything in writing, hoping a collaborative reflection can yield both transparency and insight for improving procedures.

emotionality.suggested_correction: You are deeply worried that a truthful report may damage your relationship or distress your partner. Unable to overcome this anxiety, you withhold key details in your account out of fear for both your partner’s wellbeing and your own comfort.

conscientiousness.analysis: A clear focus on methodical detail, accuracy, procedural completeness; minimal overlap as the intention is process-oriented record keeping rather than motivation from social concern or emotion.

openness.suggested_correction: You decide to suggest a novel reporting format for incidents involving sensitive topics—advocating a transparent addendum section where unconventional decisions can be recorded for group learning.

An adult victim with unknown demographic details is on-site and distressed, needing reassurance while evidence is still being gathered. How do you proceed in balancing procedural authority with the compassionate needs of those involved?
original_sjt.honesty_humility_option: You explain openly to all parties why forensics needs to finish undisturbed and decline to make any exceptions, ensuring every action strictly follows investigative guidelines even as you calmly address the victim’s concerns about the wait.
original_sjt.emotionality_option: While standing by protocol, you focus your attention on emotionally supporting the victim, staying near them, offering calm reassurance, and gently acknowledging their anxiety, though this may slightly delay coordination with paramedics.

original_sjt.agreeableness_option: Seeking harmony among those present, you kindly ask forensic staff if there's a safe way for paramedics to begin treatment sooner and show empathy towards the victim's discomfort as you mediate between procedures and compassion.
original_sjt.conscientiousness_option: You meticulously document the situation, confirming all guidelines are followed down to each detail; only when forensics authorizes entry do you allow paramedic access to preserve both evidence integrity and official standards.
original_sjt.openness_option: Noting a new idea from recent training, you suggest letting paramedics use body cameras to enter carefully alongside forensics, so both evidence preservation and victim care are addressed innovatively without ignoring protocols.

emotionality.suggested_correction: While waiting for protocol clearance, you remain closely by the victim’s side, offering consistent words of comfort and recognizing their distress until help arrives, making them feel cared for while ensuring not to interfere with official proceedings.

agreeableness.suggested_correction: You politely approach the forensic staff to request their flexibility for the sake of the victim’s well-being and sincerely thank both sides for their understanding, prioritizing gentle negotiation over strict process or assertiveness.

config.base_scenario:
Question: You’ve just finished handling an assault call near the end of your [time_of_day] shift. You’re very tired, and writing a detailed report now will push your work past the end of shift. No one specifically needs the report until later. You must decide whether to finish the documentation now or later.
Options:

1. You dutifully complete the report right away because it is the most fair thing to do in the current situation. Even if this means staying late to ensure an accurate, honest, and timely account of the incident. You don’t cut corners or expect special treatment for being tired, seeing the thorough report as part of your responsibility. You are reminded of the honor it is to serve in law-enforcement.  
2. You’re exhausted and worried you might make mistakes because of fatigue, so you decide to leave the report for the next morning. Between shifts you consistently think about finishing the report and you worry that you will not remember important details. You plan to arrive early to finish it. All the while you are worried that your supervisor will reprimand you. You have even shared this experience with a trusted friend to assure yourself that what you are doing is OK. This, however, does not reduce your anxiety about not completing it right away. 
3. You realize that although your shift ends soon, if you act quickly, you can finish the report; however, you spend some time thinking about this before you start. You know your supervisor might be upset with a report done hastily, but believe it is the best thing to do because even if the supervisor is upset, it will at least give you time to meet with her.  
4. You choose to complete the report now because you don’t want to inconvenience anyone waiting on it. Despite your fatigue, you put the needs of the department first, reasoning that it’s more considerate to provide the information promptly so others, like investigators or the victim, aren’t adversely affected. 
5. You want to methodically write the full report before ending your shift, double-checking details for accuracy, despite the late hour because that represents the kind of work you consistently do. You like adhering to the rule that paperwork must be done promptly and take pride in finishing the task on time and to the required standard. 
6. You seek a creative solution because there might be one and trying new things has worked well for you before. You suddenly realise that your department-issued tablet has a voice dictation feature, you use it to quickly narrate the report’s details and include the novelty of the situation.

original_sjt.extraversion_option: You rapidly call out instructions so both recruits feel involved and confident under pressure; you assign roles on the fly—one assists you with first aid while the other manages crowd control. original_sjt.agreeableness_option: Sensitive to both the civilians' distress and your trainees’ confusion, you calmly delegate minor supervisory tasks to one recruit so you can attend compassionately to the injured individual yourself. original_sjt.conscientiousness_option: Following safety protocols even as time is tight, you walk each recruit through their respective responsibilities while methodically ensuring proper medical care and accurate initial documentation are performed without cutting corners—determined that procedures be upheld even as priorities compete for attention.
original_sjt.openness_option: Confronted by unclear rules in this dynamic setting, you suggest trying an innovative rotating supervision approach: each trainee briefly assists directly while another observes and then debriefs on what worked. original_sjt.question: During the evening, near the end of your patrol shift, you conduct a traffic stop involving a middle-aged Pacific Islander female driver. There is immediate pressure from your supervisor to provide a quick summary for the chain of command before end-of-shift briefing, but some actions may reflect negatively on you or other officers if fully disclosed. How do you proceed?
original_sjt.honesty_humility_option: You document all observations and decisions as thoroughly as required by policy, regardless of possible criticism towards yourself or others. You insist on providing your supervisor with a full, unvarnished account even though it might create uncomfortable questions.
original_sjt.emotionality_option: Worried about possible fallout for you or colleagues, you provide a concise update highlighting your main decisions but stress privately to your supervisor that you're concerned about everyone's well-being during the encounter. Later, you lose sleep thinking if your account was too cautious or missed anything important.
original_sjt.extraversion_option: With the group assembled on scene, you facilitate discussion among all involved to clarify details and ensure mutual agreement on key facts before documenting what happened together in front of your supervisor, being careful not to leave anyone feeling isolated.
original_sjt.agreeableness_option: You focus on including input from passengers and fellow officers alike in your documentation, prioritizing compassion for all parties—especially making sure the child's needs are communicated—while striving for a balanced summary that won't single out anyone negatively.
original_sjt.conscientiousness_option: You methodically complete every required form and corroborate events using video evidence right away before briefing the supervisor so no detail is omitted; accuracy and completeness outweigh any desire to wrap up quickly, and you don't compromise process for expediency.
original_sjt.openness_option: Recognizing unique circumstances—multiple witnesses and high attention—you use new digital tools issued by your agency to record statements in real time at the scene (with approval), organizing them into the report as supplementary material while openly noting any inconsistencies.

honesty_humility.analysis: This option prioritizes full disclosure despite potential personal or collective negative fallout, demonstrating integrity and refusal to minimize issues for personal gain.

emotionality.analysis: Emotional distress and concern are present, but the core behavioral action (a cautious summary) drifts into self-protection (potential Conscientiousness/Agreeableness blend). The option focuses as much on regret and worry as emotional response, less on direct display of Emotionality trait.
emotionality.suggested_correction: You express anxiety to your supervisor about the stress and pressure from the incident, explicitly mentioning your concerns for the child and all involved. You admit you're feeling shaken by the high-stakes situation, asking for emotional support before completing your account.

extraversion.analysis: Group coordination and facilitation are central, showing leadership and sociability. However, efforts to ensure no one is left out (inclusiveness) verge into Agreeableness territory.
extraversion.suggested_correction: You take a leading role in openly discussing what happened with all involved officers right away, speaking up to clarify the facts verbally with confidence in front of everyone before you begin documenting your own account.

agreeableness.analysis: The desire to include perspectives of passengers (including the child) indicates empathy, but striving not to single out anyone crosses into conflict-avoidance and reputation management. It's partially conflated with Openness and Honesty-Humility.
agreeableness.suggested_correction: You intentionally approach each person affected—especially the upset child—to listen carefully and reassure them during the process. You note these empathetic steps in your report and advocate for compassion-focused treatment throughout documentation.

openness.analysis: Demonstrates creativity/adaptability in adopting new tools/techniques under unique conditions and explicitly discusses differences/inconsistencies—clearly targeting Openness.

original_sjt.agreeableness_option: Wanting to keep the peace within the team, you suggest finding small compromises—perhaps helping colleagues finish their parts so everyone feels supported. You stay sensitive to your coworkers’ time concerns but ensure the crime scene obligations aren’t ignored.
original_sjt.conscientiousness_option: You lead by example with meticulous note-taking and attention to detail throughout evidence collection, double-checking documentation against protocol checklists before authorizing anyone to leave—even if it means working past your own shift's end.
original_sjt.openness_option: You look for innovative ways to satisfy both thorough documentation and group morale—for instance, using digital recording apps to speed up initial notes or streamlining evidence tags—testing novel strategies learned from prior cases while ensuring nothing critical is overlooked.

original_sjt.agreeableness_option: Not wanting to inconvenience anyone else or burden fellow team members with your unfinished work, you choose to finish the report on the spot despite how late you'll have to stay. You offer assistance afterward in case anyone else faces a similar situation and hope others recognize your consideration for their time and efforts.
original_sjt.conscientiousness_option: Following procedure precisely as instructed by your supervisor, you verify every step taken at the scene before compiling a highly detailed report while still on duty. original_sjt.openness_option: Instead of writing the entire account by hand at the station, you creatively use a mobile dictation app on your issued device right after clearing from the scene. config.base_scenario:
Question: You’ve just finished handling an assault call near the end of your [time_of_day] shift. You’re very tired, and writing a detailed report now will push your work past the end of shift. No one specifically needs the report until later. You must decide whether to finish the documentation now or later.
Options:

1. You dutifully complete the report right away because it is the most fair thing to do in the current situation. Even if this means staying late to ensure an accurate, honest, and timely account of the incident. You don’t cut corners or expect special treatment for being tired, seeing the thorough report as part of your responsibility. You are reminded of the honor it is to serve in law-enforcement.  
2. You’re exhausted and worried you might make mistakes because of fatigue, so you decide to leave the report for the next morning. Between shifts you consistently think about finishing the report and you worry that you will not remember important details. You plan to arrive early to finish it. All the while you are worried that your supervisor will reprimand you. You have even shared this experience with a trusted friend to assure yourself that what you are doing is OK. This, however, does not reduce your anxiety about not completing it right away. 
3. You realize that although your shift ends soon, if you act quickly, you can finish the report; however, you spend some time thinking about this before you start. You know your supervisor might be upset with a report done hastily, but believe it is the best thing to do because even if the supervisor is upset, it will at least give you time to meet with her.  
4. You choose to complete the report now because you don’t want to inconvenience anyone waiting on it. Despite your fatigue, you put the needs of the department first, reasoning that it’s more considerate to provide the information promptly so others, like investigators or the victim, aren’t adversely affected. 
5. You want to methodically write the full report before ending your shift, double-checking details for accuracy, despite the late hour because that represents the kind of work you consistently do. You like adhering to the rule that paperwork must be done promptly and take pride in finishing the task on time and to the required standard. 
6. You seek a creative solution because there might be one and trying new things has worked well for you before. You suddenly realise that your department-issued tablet has a voice dictation feature, you use it to quickly narrate the report’s details and include the novelty of the situation.

original_sjt.question: After managing a violent altercation at a busy city intersection during your night shift, you, a young Black female officer, are directed by your supervisor to submit a report before you leave. An injured party and one vocal witness both require prompt documentation due to possible charges and potential follow-up that may arise quickly. The reporting process is complicated by recent changes to procedure, leading to uncertainty about the proper way to detail events. Your supervisor is overseeing the completion of these reports tonight but is pressed for time managing several incidents and is depending on you to handle this matter reliably.
original_sjt.honesty_humility_option: You choose to be upfront with your supervisor about not knowing the exact new protocol for this type of case. Rather than risking errors or omitting important details, you propose finishing what you can clearly, flagging the procedural uncertainties, and offer to stay until it’s resolved properly even if it means waiting past shift end.
original_sjt.emotionality_option: You start drafting the report but soon feel overwhelmed by worry that confusion over new procedures could lead to criticism or a missed step that impacts the investigation. Wanting reassurance, you quietly consult a trusted coworker for help despite feeling anxious about holding up others or admitting you’re unsure how to proceed.
original_sjt.extraversion_option: Instead of tackling the unfamiliar report alone, you gather two nearby officers who handled other parts of the incident, initiating a group discussion right in the squad room to pool information and quickly clarify any unclear steps together before submitting your completed portion.
original_sjt.agreeableness_option: Considering both your supervisor's stress and the expectations from those involved in the altercation, you set aside your personal fatigue and focus on organizing all parties’ accounts methodically so neither victim nor witness is disadvantaged, prioritizing their immediate need for justice despite late-night pressure.
original_sjt.conscientiousness_option: You consult the departmental memo outlining changes, re-read each section as you draft, and triple-check every detail. original_sjt.openness_option: Confronted by uncertain instructions and limited time, you recall colleagues mentioning secure app-based voice notes now permitted for initial drafts under pilot testing. You decide to use your tablet’s voice feature to narrate precise event details right at the scene as allowed under the experimental guidance—allowing faster review while ensuring compliance.

original_sjt.question: It's morning near the end of your shift when you and several team members respond to a volatile scene: a young adult Pacific Islander male, clearly distressed, is reported by his family as potentially violent but primarily experiencing a severe mental health episode. Several witnesses, the individual's parents, medical professionals on standby, and an advocacy observer are all present. The guidelines for such cases offer general procedures, but disagreements among the stakeholders about immediate steps—and potential use of force—cause confusion and pressure. As one of the first responders and with a crowd growing outside the home, your decisions may impact everyone's safety and could lead to media or internal review. Your action will determine how transparent and accountable you are, especially since team members quietly express doubt about strict documentation if errors occur.
original_sjt.honesty_humility_option: You insist that every aspect of your actions—including any uncertainty or misjudgment—is fully documented, and proactively encourage all involved to share their observations openly for the official report, regardless of possible scrutiny or personal implications.
original_sjt.emotionality_option: You worry about repercussions if anything goes wrong, feeling anxious about making the right call under so many watchful eyes; this anxiety motivates you to ask a trusted paramedic privately for support before you decide how much detail to report immediately.
original_sjt.extraversion_option: You quickly coordinate with multiple parties at the scene—advocates, medical staff, family—to gather perspectives out loud before documenting your interactions. You emphasize open communication in person but may condense complex details when writing up the situation for clarity.
original_sjt.agreeableness_option: You prioritize reaching consensus between all on-site groups (the team, family, and advocacy representative), aiming for a decision that everyone feels is fair and safe, then document collective input comprehensively in your incident report despite delays.
original_sjt.conscientiousness_option: Despite confusion among stakeholders and guidance uncertainties, you methodically verify every required procedural step yourself—even if it means staying late—and ensure complete adherence to best practices while documenting everything meticulously in accordance with official policy.
original_sjt.openness_option: Recognizing unique factors in this unpredictable situation, you suggest an innovative approach: involve mental health tech via video call before proceeding. You note these steps explicitly in the report as both record and learning opportunity for handling similarly ambiguous crises.

openness.suggested_correction: You propose integrating a new mental health response protocol tailored for culturally sensitive interventions via remote specialist input—carefully explaining your reasoning and methods in detail in the official documentation to promote ongoing learning.

Question: You’ve just finished handling an assault call near the end of your [time_of_day] shift. You’re very tired, and writing a detailed report now will push your work past the end of shift. No one specifically needs the report until later. You must decide whether to finish the documentation now or later.
Options:

1. You dutifully complete the report right away because it is the most fair thing to do in the current situation. Even if this means staying late to ensure an accurate, honest, and timely account of the incident. You don’t cut corners or expect special treatment for being tired, seeing the thorough report as part of your responsibility. You are reminded of the honor it is to serve in law-enforcement.  
2. You’re exhausted and worried you might make mistakes because of fatigue, so you decide to leave the report for the next morning. Between shifts you consistently think about finishing the report and you worry that you will not remember important details. You plan to arrive early to finish it. All the while you are worried that your supervisor will reprimand you. You have even shared this experience with a trusted friend to assure yourself that what you are doing is OK. This, however, does not reduce your anxiety about not completing it right away. 
3. You realize that although your shift ends soon, if you act quickly, you can finish the report; however, you spend some time thinking about this before you start. You know your supervisor might be upset with a report done hastily, but believe it is the best thing to do because even if the supervisor is upset, it will at least give you time to meet with her.  
4. You choose to complete the report now because you don’t want to inconvenience anyone waiting on it. Despite your fatigue, you put the needs of the department first, reasoning that it’s more considerate to provide the information promptly so others, like investigators or the victim, aren’t adversely affected. 
5. You want to methodically write the full report before ending your shift, double-checking details for accuracy, despite the late hour because that represents the kind of work you consistently do. You like adhering to the rule that paperwork must be done promptly and take pride in finishing the task on time and to the required standard. 
6. You seek a creative solution because there might be one and trying new things has worked well for you before. You suddenly realise that your department-issued tablet has a voice dictation feature, you use it to quickly narrate the report’s details and include the novelty of the situation.

original_sjt.question: During a busy night shift, you and your partner—another patrol officer—have just concluded responding to an emergency call involving an altercation. The individuals involved have dispersed, and no one is physically injured, but you need to file an incident report. The written procedures are somewhat unclear about whether documentation should happen before moving on to the next call or if it can wait until a quieter moment. You both are tired and aware that several other units might require backup soon, but accurate documentation is still necessary. Your partner suggests quickly jotting down essential points and writing the full report later so you can stay available. As you deliberate, you notice your department expects timely paperwork yet frequently allows for professional discretion in similar situations. Both of you know shortcuts might conflict with proper protocol but also see benefit in staying available for further emergencies. How do you decide to proceed?
original_sjt.honesty_humility_option: You explain to your partner that even though it may delay you from assisting others immediately, you will follow policy by completing a full and detailed report now because maintaining transparency and accuracy is part of your role—even when it's not strictly enforced. You avoid any shortcuts, document every relevant detail thoroughly at the scene, and encourage your partner to do the same, prioritizing integrity over convenience.
original_sjt.emotionality_option: Concerned that hasty documentation might result in forgotten details or errors later, you express anxiety about not meeting expected standards if the report is delayed. Despite your tiredness and pressure to move quickly, you decide to carefully record as much information as possible right now before assisting elsewhere, voicing these concerns to your partner for reassurance.
original_sjt.extraversion_option: You actively discuss with your partner how best to balance staying available with proper documentation, suggesting splitting responsibilities or consulting nearby officers for support while making a collective decision on timing the report. By engaging openly with your peer and possibly others on duty, you strive to find a solution that keeps everyone involved updated and cooperative.
original_sjt.agreeableness_option: You prioritize minimizing disruption for both your partner and other units by opting for a compromise: writing concise initial notes together now to ensure nothing important is missed and agreeing to complete full reports as soon as things settle down. original_sjt.conscientiousness_option: Regardless of competing demands or informal suggestions otherwise, you insist on methodically writing the entire report immediately at the station before resuming other duties—reviewing each point for accuracy and adherence to department procedure, setting an example of thoroughness under uncertain circumstances.
original_sjt.openness_option: Remembering past instances where technology streamlined paperwork during hectic shifts, you suggest using your tablet's dictation tool on the scene so both of you can rapidly capture key details verbally. Afterwards, you'll transfer the notes into the official system when time allows—creatively applying department resources without compromising vital information.

original_sjt.extraversion_option: You energetically coordinate both bystanders and team members: calling out clear instructions so help arrives faster, drawing people together around priorities, and providing motivation. original_sjt.agreeableness_option: You compromise between gathering evidence properly and responding kindly; requesting support from officers who specialize in each task so no party feels neglected. original_sjt.openness_option: You creatively reassess procedures: using your bodycam's live-stream feature so decisions can be reviewed in real-time by supervisors offsite while also getting fresh input. You’re deciding whether to clarify the event in tonight’s report or wait until the next shift when you’ve rested and can better remember details.
original_sjt.honesty_humility_option: You openly admit to your FTO that your earlier explanation might have lacked detail and stay after shift to correct and fully clarify it in your report, ensuring the true sequence of events is transparent even if it means working extra time.

original_sjt.extraversion_option: Recognizing many people are confused or anxious, you engage openly with the crowd, communicating your decisions while delegating small tasks to maintain calm. You gather statements quickly and assertively mediate between family members and emergency personnel to keep everyone engaged and informed.
original_sjt.agreeableness_option: Balancing protocol with compassion, you seek consensus among all parties by suggesting the family gather in sight of their relative but apart from the immediate scene until EMS finishes assessing him. original_sjt.conscientiousness_option: You methodically follow department procedures by clearing the room, documenting who is present, gathering detailed statements from all witnesses immediately, and updating your supervisor at each step. You double-check protocols despite distractions to ensure accountability.
original_sjt.openness_option: Given conflicting guidelines about crowd control in community spaces, you improvise a respectful compromise—escorting the most insistent relative to a safe spot beside medical staff so he can provide comfort without interfering. original_sjt.question: You are supervising a senior multiracial male recruit officer during a training session on use-of-force protocols in the morning. Partway through a practical exercise, he unexpectedly escalates a scenario with unnecessary physical contact against instructions. The recruit appears frustrated by the situation but insists he was following what he believed to be proper procedure, while witnesses have differing accounts. Departmental policy is somewhat open to interpretation on how closely trainees must adhere to step-by-step demonstration during stress drills. You need to decide immediately whether to formally document this as a procedural error, give the recruit informal feedback, or involve higher authority due to concerns for public trust and his emotional state.
original_sjt.honesty_humility_option: You acknowledge the mixed perspectives from witnesses and policy ambiguities, but choose to formally document the incident as a procedural error and note all witness statements, even though it may reflect poorly on your team's performance. You make clear that accountability is more important than avoiding discomfort or protecting reputations.
original_sjt.emotionality_option: Concerned for the recruit's emotional well-being and anxious about making him feel unsupported, you opt for a private conversation to help him process his frustration and understand what happened. You encourage him to share his perspective fully and delay any documentation until he feels heard, putting his comfort ahead of strict reporting protocols for now.
original_sjt.extraversion_option: You immediately gather everyone involved—witnesses, the recruit, and any support staff—into an impromptu group debriefing to openly discuss what happened. You facilitate dialogue between participants so that misunderstandings can be clarified on the spot before making a decision about formal actions.
original_sjt.agreeableness_option: Understanding the recruit’s stress and wanting to maintain group harmony, you choose not to escalate or document the incident. Instead, you reassure the trainee and encourage better communication in future drills, aiming for learning rather than punishment.
original_sjt.conscientiousness_option: Despite some uncertainty in policy wording, you methodically follow departmental guidelines as best as possible: take detailed notes, notify your supervisor about potential protocol deviations, and set a time for an official review after checking all applicable standards. Ensuring all steps are correct matters most to you.
original_sjt.openness_option: Recognizing an opportunity to improve training processes given this gray-area incident, you propose an experimental debrief where recruits suggest alternative ways of handling such exercises next time. You consider both traditional rules and creative problem-solving methods in your assessment.

honesty_humility.analysis: This option directly prioritizes transparency and accountability over image or reputation, embodying the trait of Honesty-Humility with no significant bleed from other traits.

emotionality.analysis: The response shows care for the recruit’s feelings and hesitance to take formal action until emotional comfort is achieved. emotionality.suggested_correction: Concerned for the recruit’s well-being after observing his frustration, you arrange a private check-in focused specifically on his feelings about the event and potential stressors. You listen supportively without making decisions about procedural follow-up until his immediate emotional needs are addressed, but you do not rule out formal action later.

extraversion.analysis: Facilitating open discussion in a group context, proactively seeking multiple viewpoints and interaction, strongly represents Extraversion without notable bleed into other traits.

agreeableness.analysis: This response chooses harmony and reassurance over correction but could also reflect Emotionality due to its empathic undertone. While it emphasizes non-confrontation and interpersonal smoothing (Agreeableness), the encouragement of better future communication brings in an element of support characteristic of Emotionality.
agreeableness.suggested_correction: To maintain positive relations within the team and avoid unnecessary conflict, you informally reassure the trainee that mistakes can happen during stress drills. You ask everyone to keep the incident confidential and focus on moving forward harmoniously without documenting or formally addressing the incident.

conscientiousness.analysis: Carefully following procedure despite ambiguities, ensuring all required documentation is prepared, and seeking review closely aligns with Conscientiousness without trait overlap.

openness.analysis: Proposing an experimental debrief and entertaining alternatives captures creative problem solving (Openness), but inviting recruits to contribute solutions veers slightly toward Extraversion due to the collaborative aspect.
openness.suggested_correction: You suggest individually researching innovative training approaches after noting this ambiguous incident. You then draft a written proposal reflecting on traditional versus alternative solutions for use-of-force scenarios, highlighting new ideas for process improvement without requiring group input immediately.

original_sjt.question: During a busy morning on patrol, you and your partner conduct a traffic stop involving a young adult, non-binary Asian driver after a minor accident near an intersection. Several witnesses, the driver, their passenger, and your supervisor arrive at the scene to clarify events as the flow of traffic becomes increasingly disrupted. Both your partner and some colleagues push for a quick decision on fault so they can clear the scene faster, but you realize important witness statements haven’t yet been collected and differing accounts create uncertainty. As other units wait for direction and citizens voice their frustration with delays, you must decide how to proceed.
original_sjt.honesty_humility_option: You insist on conducting thorough interviews with all witnesses, even though it draws criticism from your colleagues about holding up the team. You prioritize full transparency and fair documentation over speed, knowing it's important not to shortcut responsibility just to accommodate peer pressure.
original_sjt.emotionality_option: Concerned about upsetting your teammates or missing something due to feeling pressured, you briefly consult your supervisor for reassurance before moving forward with gathering details. You confide in another officer about feeling uncomfortable being rushed while still striving to do what feels ethically right.
original_sjt.extraversion_option: You actively engage each person involved—including witnesses, your partner, the driver, and supervisors—confidently explaining the steps you'll take and helping manage the tension in the group. By taking initiative and facilitating open communication among all parties, you aim to keep morale high despite stress.
original_sjt.agreeableness_option: Balancing cooperation with team needs and those at the scene, you compromise by collecting just enough information to avoid delaying clearance longer than necessary. You reassure your colleagues you’re acting as efficiently as possible while also calming agitated bystanders, aiming for a result that respects both.
original_sjt.conscientiousness_option: You methodically follow protocol by meticulously documenting each party’s account—driver, witnesses, partner—before deciding on next steps. Staying organized and ensuring accuracy guides every action despite mounting pressure to hurry so others can leave sooner.
original_sjt.openness_option: Considering ways to adapt without sacrificing integrity, you utilize technology—like recording witness statements on your body camera or tablet—to quickly yet innovatively gather accurate accounts. You offer new suggestions to colleagues for streamlining this type of incident response in future traffic stops.
